look_here_first: CAROLINA CANARYGRASS (maygrass): look for a fairly firm, dense, oval-to-elongate light-green head with overlapping pointed, faintly green-and-pale-striped glumes, above flat shiny leaves on an ANNUAL grass. The true test is ONE dissected 4–6 mm spikelet: two narrow, hairy REDUCED STERILE florets below one fertile floret, surrounded by two keeled, narrowly winged glumes. Introduced lesser canarygrass (Phalaris minor) has ONE reduced sterile floret; head shape, flowering color and site moisture are insufficient by themselves. FIVE source-labelled physically archived Harms photos now show whole annual habit, entire flowering head, compact inflorescence details, individual spikelet, and photographed collar/sheath. They do NOT yet independently prove individual TWO inner sterile lemmas; count those in a dissected mature spikelet with true 1mm ruler. Original attribution copyrighted science/education, not CC.

best_field_traits: Annual fibrous-rooted, usually several erect/ascending tillers (not a persistent rhizomatous Phalaris colony).
Panicle dense and spikelike, often ovoid to subcylindrical, about 0.5–8 cm long and 0.8–2 cm wide; green, pale-striped overlapping outer glumes, awnless.

Spikelets strongly flattened side to side, about 3.8–6 mm; two similar sharply keeled glumes with narrow distal wings, typically entire; do not label individual wing edges from an unmeasured group photo.
Decisive mature dissection: TWO hairy reduced sterile florets roughly 1.5–2.5 mm long plus ONE fertile floret, unlike P. minor's ONE reduced sterile floret.
True leaf ligule is a translucent membrane, often 1.5–7 mm, best measured in a sharp collar macro; no reliable photo of this structure yet.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Full rooted spring grass with fibrous annual roots, multiple leafy culms, intact seedhead and an actual ruler
Same-shoot leaf sheath/blade junction showing pale membranous ligule measured with 1-mm scale
One mature detached and OPENED Phalaris caroliniana spikelet, both lateral sides, individually labeled two narrow sterile lemmas and fertile floret with scale
Compare to a confirmed P. minor spikelet with exactly ONE sterile lemma and toothed/erose glume wing in matching magnification
Mat-like fluffy Polypogon monspeliensis foxtail head, with visible awns contrasted against the layered Phalaris head (no false counts from distant photographs)
crew_field_check: At first glance look for a tight green, firm, rather ovoid canarygrass seedhead with sharp overlapping glumes instead of the longer fluffy awn-bearing bottlebrush of Polypogon.
Locate the entire plant base and collar: Carolina canarygrass is a cool-season annual with a membranous ligule; season and damp site are supporting, not decisive.
Separate P. minor from P. caroliniana at magnification by counting reduced STERILE FLORETS inside ONE opened spikelet: ONE in introduced P. minor versus TWO in Carolina canarygrass.
Check P. canariensis: another introduced annual with TWO sterile florets but considerably broader conspicuous glume wings and often larger glumes; do not confuse broad wing with the sterile lemmas.

Check narrow panicles against native P. angusta (two shorter reduced florets, generally narrower cylindrical panicle) and rhizomatous perennial P. arundinacea; both require site/range verification and dissection.
Do not reclassify unknown canarygrass as native based on one photo, nor change Hays county nativity metrics.

comparisons.key_distinctions: P. minor is the dangerous look-alike: similarly firm compact canarygrass head, usually one sterile floret (vs two in Carolina); P. minor's glume wings are often irregularly dentate, Carolina usually smoother/entire but variable. P. canariensis ALSO has two sterile florets: its glumes are markedly broader, typically 7–10 mm, with more obvious wings. P. angusta is generally more narrowly cylindrical and has shorter reduced sterile florets (~0.7–1.5 mm vs Carolina 1.5–2.5 mm). Polypogon monspeliensis has fine long awns giving a soft fuzzy head. P. arundinacea is perennial/rhizomatous with potentially spreading flowering branches; annual rooted base confirms against that species.

visual_comparison.title: CAROLINA CANARYGRASS — recognize the head, then count sterile florets
visual_comparison.subtitle: CURRENT SIX teaching panels: five actual archived Bob Harms Phalaris caroliniana photographs (mounted flowering specimen, entire head, head detail, dissected spikelet plate, collar region) plus ONE explicitly DIFFERENT-SPECIES Phalaris minor CC BY 2.0 head reference. Six local same-species photo records also include a legacy Andy Newman CC BY-NC original NOT displayed in these panels. Bob Harms images are copyrighted with credited educational-use terms, NOT Creative Commons; local-copy and annotation scope needs separate verification. Neither the two distinct sterile lemmas nor a measured free ligule edge has yet been certified from these photos.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: CAROLINA: TWO reduced sterile florets + one fertile inside paired keeled glumes. MINOR: ONE reduced sterile floret. The green dense head is a clue, NOT confirmation.

diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.look_here_first: Dense light-green, sometimes striped ovoid head on a fibrous-rooted ANNUAL; definitive test is one dissected mature spikelet with TWO narrow reduced sterile florets below ONE fertile floret. diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.growth_form: Tufted annual, without rhizomes; dense spikelike panicle around 1–7 cm long in Kew treatment. Head shape alone cannot certify species.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.ligule_collar: True eciliate membranous ligule, 1–7 mm in Flora Neomexicana; auricles absent. Show blade/sheath junction and actual membrane beside ruler, not only sheath edge.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.spikelet_glume_lemma_awn: UT Williamson treatment: mature spikelet glumes 4.8–5.3 mm, three-veined and narrowly winged along keels; TWO reduced sterile lemmas approximately 1.5–2 mm; fertile lemma approximately 3.5 mm and hairy; fertile palea approximately 2 mm. All florets awnless. Kew reports spikelets 4.2–5.6 mm and fertile lemmas 3–4.7 mm; local ranges vary.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
field_id_short_tiles.short: A compact, firm, green canarygrass head—not a fluffy awned foxtail
field_id_short_tiles.details: Actual archived Bob Harms whole flowering-specimen panel 1 shows several attached leafy shoots and panicles; panel 2 displays the entire dense short-branched seedhead; panel 3 magnifies overlapping glumes. A contracted ovoid to cylindrical head is a first clue (FNA 0.5–8 cm long, often 0.8–2 cm wide), but several introduced Phalaris look similar. The one- vs two-STERILE-LEMMA difference cannot be determined from head silhouette alone.
field_id_short_tiles.status: COMPLETE ATTACHED HEAD VISIBLE; SPECIES-LEVEL DISSECTION STILL NECESSARY

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · FOLLOW THE ROOTED ANNUAL
field_id_short_tiles.short: Annual bunchgrass; exposed fibrous roots still missing
field_id_short_tiles.details: This is a spring/cool-season annual, not a rhizomatous reed canarygrass colony. The archived mounted whole flowering specimen (panel 1) includes several basal culms, but roots are outside the visible image. Williamson County's detailed flora specifies fibrous-rooted, 1–several stems at base, NOT rosetted. Do not confuse the familiar pale compressed goosegrass crown with maygrass. Next field photo must show a properly identified attached stem, actual roots and the central crown with a centimeter scale.
field_id_short_tiles.status: WHOLE FLOWERING HABIT PHOTOGRAPHED; ROOT SYSTEM NOT PHOTOGRAPHED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE TWO GLUMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: A ~4–6 mm spikelet enclosed by two narrowly winged glumes
field_id_short_tiles.details: Actual source photos (panels 3 and 4) show sharply keeled outer glumes. Flora of North America gives glumes about 3.8–6(8) mm, varying slightly with geography; the Williamson County detailed treatment gives roughly 4.8–5.3 mm with narrow keel wings. An image's generic black-white strip is NOT sufficient for a measured value until the original scale's physical units are documented. Isolate one ripe spikelet, photograph both glumes, and place a true millimeter ruler alongside.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED DIMENSIONS; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — SEPARATED MEASURED GLUMES

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · COUNT THE REDUCED STERILE FLORETS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Two WELL-DEVELOPED reduced sterile lemmas; one fertile floret
field_id_short_tiles.details: Carolina canarygrass contains TWO distinguishable narrow sterile lemmas below a single fertile floret, commonly around 1.5–2.5 mm. Bob Harms's dissected spikelet composite (panel 4) shows opened floral structures but does NOT resolve and label each small sterile lemma unambiguously. Importantly, lesser canarygrass P. minor usually has ONE conspicuous sterile lemma plus another absent or VERY TINY vestige (~0.3 mm); some treatments count this vestige as a second sterile floret. So don't teach absolute 'two versus one total' without explaining the vestige. Match actual side-by-side dissected spikelets and measure both sterile lemmas separately. EXTRA ACTUAL GENUS-LEVEL PHOTO MODEL (panel 8): a separately photographed, source-authenticated P. arundinacea spikelet has the two thin reduced sterile lemmas visibly separated with a real 5-mm scale. THIS IS NOT P. CAROLINIANA and does not fill our species-specific dissection hold.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL OTHER-SPECIES ANATOMY TEACHING MODEL ADDED; EXACT P. CAROLINIANA TWO-LEMMA DISSECTION STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · OPEN THE TRUE LEAF COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Membranous ligule, not a tuft of hairs
field_id_short_tiles.details: Bob Harms's true leaf junction plate (panel 5) already provides more than a vague head photo: pale blade/sheath lips and adjacent alternating dark/pale scale markings are visible. A true eciliate membrane is described for P. caroliniana (FNA usually 1.5–7 mm; Williamson County ~1–6.5 mm), not a hairs-only ligule. The free edge and original plate scale-unit calibration have not been demonstrated in this archived image. Do NOT arrow a sheath lip as the full ligule, or read precise mm from unverified bars. Photograph a peeled INNER junction with a labelled 1-mm rule.
field_id_short_tiles.status: ACTUAL COLLAR PHOTO WITH SCALE GRAPHIC; FREE EDGE/UNITS STILL UNVERIFIED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · RULE OUT LESSER CANARYGRASS
field_id_short_tiles.short: P. minor often has one obvious sterile lemma plus vestige
field_id_short_tiles.details: The current P. minor photo (panel 0) is a correctly distinguished OTHER-SPECIES whole head, not a matched floret dissection. P. caroliniana: two recognizable narrow reduced sterile lemmas typically 1.5–2.5 mm, glume keels narrowly winged. P. minor: usually one developed sterile lemma around 0.7–1.8 mm, with a second vestigial scale about 0.3 mm or absent; the glume wing often irregularly toothed. Crucial nuance: some botanical treatments count P. minor's minute scale and report TWO basal sterile florets; so compare DEVELOPMENT, not simply a hard yes/no floret tally. Introduced P. canariensis ALSO has two substantial sterile lemmas, but usually longer and broader glumes; native P. angusta can likewise have two but often shorter sterile structures. Use an opened mature spikelet, never head color or anther hue alone.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PRECISE OTHER-SPECIES COMPARISON; VERIFIED MM DISSECTION STILL PENDING

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: How to identify Carolina canarygrass (Phalaris caroliniana) — field crew
steps: 1 · SEEDHEAD — View the Bob Harms whole head (teaching panel 2) and gross overlapping-glume macro (panel 3). Both are original source-identified species photos. The compact oblong-to-ovoid contracted panicle is an excellent field clue but not enough alone to separate P. minor.

2 · GROWTH BASE — Trace the attached basal leaves and flowering culms of the mounted plant (panel 1). The ROOTS ARE NOT EXPOSED. Locate a live plant and lift an intact fibrous-root crown; annual maygrass is not a persistent rhizomatous reed canarygrass colony.

3 · TRUE LIGULE — Compare the source-labelled leaf/sheath junction plate (panel 5). Find the INSIDE blade/sheath boundary, then gently peel back the blade. Published ligule is a membrane, not a hair fringe. The pictured alternating scale marks lack independently verified unit calibration here.
4 · SPIKELET — Use panels 3 and 4 to recognize broad keeled glumes and a compact enclosed central floret. Extract one mature unit, retain both glumes, and dissect the contents with a real 1-mm ruler.

5 · DIAGNOSTIC STERILE LEMMAS — Identify two separate narrow reduced sterile lemmas at the base of the sole bisexual floret in P. caroliniana; P. minor usually has one obvious sterile lemma and either a microscopic second scale or none. Existing pictures don't establish both free edges with arrow certainty.

6 · LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES — Keep P. minor photo panel 0 explicitly tagged DIFFERENT species. Also compare P. canariensis, P. angusta, and rhizomatous P. arundinacea; complete plant habitat plus opened ripe spikelet are needed before species-level claims.
